country.name: Argentina
country.summary: Argentina grows its wine in a desert. Nearly every vineyard lies in the rain shadow of the Andes, strung along the eastern foothills from Jujuy and Salta, close to the Tropic of Capricorn, to Chubut in Patagonia, and nearly every vine drinks snowmelt led along canals. Altitude stands in for latitude: the north plants mostly from about 1,500 to over 3,000 metres, Mendoza at roughly 600 to over 1,500, Patagonia low and cool in the south. Mendoza holds most of the vineyard, and Malbec, the French grape introduced in 1853, is the national grape: dark, plush and violet scented in Luján de Cuyo, tauter and more floral from the Uco Valley. Torrontés is the white, perfumed yet dry, at its best in Cafayate. Labels work by grape and place: 85 per cent of a named variety, a geographic indication, and a DOC tier held by Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael.
country.overview:
Vines came with Spanish priests in the middle of the sixteenth century, crossing from Chile and Peru. Mendoza was founded from Chile in 1561 and San Juan the year after, and for three centuries the vineyard meant the Criolla grapes: the Listán Prieto that Argentina calls Criolla Chica, and its pink-skinned offspring. The French varieties arrived in 1853, when the agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget planted a collection of cuttings, Malbec among them, at the new provincial agricultural school in Mendoza; 17 April, the date in 1853 of the provincial measure founding the school, is now Malbec World Day. The railway reached Mendoza from Buenos Aires in 1885 and brought Italian and Spanish immigrants who planted for a vast home market of cheap, plentiful wine. The turn came in the 1990s: foreign investment, French oak and a search for higher, cooler ground, led by Catena's Adrianna vineyard at Gualtallary, planted in 1992. Malbec became the export story of the 2000s.

The vineyard is a ribbon along the eastern foot of the Andes from about 22 to about 45 degrees south. Pacific weather drops its rain on Chile, so the Argentine side is dry: Mendoza sees around 200 millimetres a year, most of it in summer storms, and San Juan less. Water comes from the mountains through rivers, dams, the old acequia canals and, more and more, drip lines. Sun is constant, fungal disease rare, and most vines grow on their own roots, because phylloxera, though present, struggles in sand and under flood irrigation. The hazards are hail, which can strip a vineyard in minutes and explains the nets over the best sites; the Zonda, a hot, dry wind that falls off the Andes in late winter and spring; and spring frost on the highest ground. Altitude is the grower's thermostat: every hundred metres up costs roughly six tenths of a degree, and the thin air brings stronger ultraviolet light, thicker skins and wider swings between day and night.

Wines of Argentina divides the country into the North (Jujuy, Salta, Catamarca, Tucumán), Cuyo (La Rioja, San Juan, Mendoza), Patagonia (Neuquén, Río Negro, La Pampa, Chubut) and a small Atlantic fringe in Buenos Aires province. The INV, the national wine institute created by law in 1959, regulates it all. Ley 25.163 of 1999 set three tiers of origin: the Indicación de Procedencia for table and regional wine, the Indicación Geográfica for quality wine from a delimited area, and the Denominación de Origen Controlada, which adds the zone's own rules. Luján de Cuyo, recognised in 1989, and San Rafael are the DOCs a server meets; the IG is the working tier, from whole provinces down to soil-mapped districts such as Paraje Altamira. A named grape or vintage must reach 85 per cent.

The exam leans on Malbec and its 1853 arrival, Luján de Cuyo against the Uco Valley, the effect of altitude, Torrontés and its three types, Bonarda's true identity, the Zonda and hail, and Patagonia as the cool, low exception.
ladder: The top tier of Ley 25.163, with rules of grape, yield and ageing set by the zone. Luján de Cuyo, recognised in 1989 and built around Malbec, and San Rafael in southern Mendoza are the two a server meets; few labels print either.
Quality wine from a delimited area: a province, a department, a valley or a soil-mapped district such as Paraje Altamira, Los Chacayes or San Pablo. The working tier of Argentine labels.
The origin statement for table and regional wine; a broad name and few demands.
Wine with no stated origin, much of it from Criolla Grande, Cereza and Pedro Giménez for the home market.
A named grape variety or a stated vintage must account for at least 85 per cent of the wine.
labels: Bodega
Winery; the first word of most houses' names.
Finca
Estate or vineyard, often a single named site; no legal rank.
Paraje
A named spot or district; Paraje Altamira is an IG, but the word itself carries no legal weight.
Corte
A blend, usually of grapes; Malbec with Cabernet Sauvignon is the classic red corte.
Viñas viejas
Old vines; an unregulated term.
Reserva, Gran Reserva
Lightly regulated words that suggest longer ageing; not Rioja's strict ladder.
Altura
Vineyard altitude in metres above sea level, printed as a climate cue; no legal classification.
Cosecha
Vintage; 85 per cent of the wine must come from the stated year.
Cosecha tardía
Late harvest: a sweet wine, often from Torrontés.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: The national grape, introduced in 1853: dark, plush and violet scented, finest from Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley, inky in Salta and red fruited in Patagonia.

grapes.name: Bonarda
grapes.styles: The Douce Noire of Savoie and, in the 2020s, the second most planted red after Malbec: soft, juicy and purple, the everyday red of East Mendoza and San Juan.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripe cassis and herb, made on its own and blended with Malbec in the great houses' cortes.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: San Juan's calling card, warm, ripe and spicy from the Tulum Valley, fresher from the high western valleys.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: The rising red of the Uco Valley, herbal and floral, bottled alone and in blends.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Patagonia's pride, pale and spicy, and a sparkling base in the high Uco Valley.

grapes.name: Torrontés
grapes.styles: Argentina's own white, in three varieties: Riojano, Sanjuanino and Mendocino, with Riojano making the perfumed, dry wines of Cafayate and La Rioja.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The leading quality white, saline and taut from Gualtallary, rounder lower down, and the base of Mendoza's traditional-method sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Criolla Chica
grapes.styles: Listán Prieto, the mission grape Chile calls País; once the vineyard's backbone, now revived for light, fresh reds from old vines.

grapes.name: Cereza
grapes.styles: Pink skinned and high yielding, with Criolla Grande the bulk of the old domestic vineyard; everyday wine, juice and concentrate.

grapes.name: Pedro Giménez
grapes.styles: A widely planted white for bulk wine and concentrate in Mendoza and San Juan; not Spain's Pedro Ximénez.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: Old vines in the Uco Valley, San Rafael and Río Negro, rediscovered for waxy, textured whites.

exam: Malbec: introduced in 1853 by the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget, now the national grape; 17 April is Malbec World Day.
Tie each style to its address: Luján de Cuyo for classic Malbec, the Uco Valley for high, floral Malbec and Chardonnay, Cafayate for Torrontés, San Juan for Syrah, Patagonia for Pinot Noir.
Know the law's three tiers, IP, IG and DOC, the two DOCs and the 85 per cent rule for variety and vintage.
Explain altitude: cooler temperatures, stronger ultraviolet light, thicker skins and a wide swing between day and night.
Name the hazards: the Zonda wind, summer hail and spring frost, and the snowmelt irrigation that makes the desert farmable.
Know the grapes' identities: Bonarda is Douce Noire, and Torrontés Riojano is Muscat of Alexandria crossed with Criolla Chica.
traps: Argentina's La Rioja is a province, not Spain's Rioja; it grows Torrontés and Malbec, not Tempranillo.
Bonarda here is Savoie's Douce Noire, California's Charbono; it is not Piedmont's Bonarda or the Croatina sold as Bonarda in Lombardy.
Argentine Torrontés is unrelated to the Torrontés of Galicia's Ribeiro, and it smells sweet but is usually dry.
Reserva on an Argentine label promises little; it is not the Spanish ageing tier.
Altitude on a label is a climate cue, not a classification; neither IG nor DOC ranks height.
Argentine Spanish says ll and y as a soft zh: Valle de Uco is VAH-zhay day OO-ko, Luján de Cuyo loo-HAHN day KOO-zho.
Patagonia's vineyards are low, at a few hundred metres; their coolness comes from latitude and wind, not altitude.

cards.f: Argentina's law of origin: the three tiers
cards.b: Ley 25.163 of 1999: Indicación de Procedencia (table and regional wine), Indicación Geográfica (quality wine of a delimited area, the working tier), Denominación de Origen Controlada (Luján de Cuyo, San Rafael).

1853: the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget planted French varieties, Malbec among them, at Mendoza's new agricultural school. 17 April, the date of the 1853 provincial measure founding the school, is Malbec World Day.
Roughly six tenths of a degree cooler per hundred metres, stronger ultraviolet light for thicker, darker skins, and a wide day to night swing that keeps acidity.

cards.f: The four wine zones of Argentina
cards.b: The North (Jujuy, Salta, Catamarca, Tucumán), Cuyo (La Rioja, San Juan, Mendoza), Patagonia (Neuquén, Río Negro, La Pampa, Chubut) and the Atlantic coast of Buenos Aires.
The Douce Noire of Savoie, Charbono in California; in the 2020s Argentina's second most planted red after Malbec. Not Piedmont's Bonarda, nor Lombardy's Croatina.
Riojano (the finest and most perfumed), Sanjuanino and Mendocino. Riojano and Sanjuanino are Muscat of Alexandria crossed with Criolla Chica.
85 per cent for a named grape variety and 85 per cent for a stated vintage.
A hot, dry foehn that falls off the Andes, mostly in late winter and spring; it can scorch shoots and ruin flowering in Mendoza and San Juan.
The INV, Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura, created by law in 1959 and based in Mendoza.

questions.q: In which year did Michel Aimé Pouget bring Malbec to Mendoza's agricultural school?
questions.exp: Michel Aimé Pouget planted Malbec at Mendoza's agricultural school in 1853. The railway reached Mendoza in 1885, Catena was founded in 1902 and Chandon came to Mendoza in 1959.

questions.q: Which grape is Argentine Bonarda, according to DNA profiling?
questions.exp: Argentine Bonarda is the Douce Noire of Savoie, the Charbono of California. Croatina is sold as Bonarda in Lombardy's Oltrepò Pavese, Bonarda Piemontese is a separate Piedmontese grape, and Dolcetto is unrelated.

questions.q: What minimum share of a wine must a named grape variety reach under Argentine rules?
questions.exp: INV rules ask 85 per cent for a named variety and the same for a stated vintage, ten points stricter than Chile's 75 per cent.

questions.q: Which national body regulates Argentine wine?
questions.exp: The Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura, created by law in 1959, controls Argentine wine from Mendoza. INAVI is Uruguay's institute, the SAG Chile's agricultural service and the OIV the international organisation.

questions.q: Which hot, dry wind descends the eastern Andes onto the vineyards of Mendoza and San Juan?
questions.exp: The Zonda is a foehn wind, warmed and dried as it falls off the Andes, most often in late winter and spring. The Pampero is a cold pampas wind, the Mistral blows down the Rhône and the Sirocco crosses the Mediterranean from Africa.

questions.q: Which Mendoza department became Argentina's first DOC in 1989?
questions.exp: Luján de Cuyo, the historic Malbec heartland just south of Mendoza city, took the first DOC in 1989; San Rafael in southern Mendoza holds the other.

questions.q: Which Spanish word on an Argentine label means a blend?
questions.exp: Corte means a blend, most often Malbec with Cabernet Sauvignon. Cosecha means vintage, finca an estate or vineyard, and paraje a named spot or district, such as Paraje Altamira.

regions.name: Salta / Cafayate
regions.summary: Salta is the far north of Argentine wine, and Cafayate, a town at about 1,700 metres in the south of the Calchaquí Valleys, is its centre. Here, not far south of the Tropic of Capricorn, altitude alone makes viticulture possible: hot, brilliant days, cold nights and fierce ultraviolet light. Torrontés Riojano is the signature, a white that smells of roses, jasmine and peach yet finishes dry, often with a faint bitter twist. The reds, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Tannat, are inky, thick skinned and firm. Up the valley, through Molinos and Cachi to Payogasta, the vineyards climb past 3,000 metres, among the highest anywhere.

terroir.climate: A high desert under a subtropical sun. Cafayate receives under 200 millimetres of rain a year, nearly all of it in brief summer storms, and the air is so dry that rot is almost unknown. Days in the ripening season are hot and nights cold, and the daily swing can reach twenty degrees or more. Altitude cuts the heat the latitude would otherwise bring and strengthens the ultraviolet light, which the vines answer with thicker, darker skins. Afternoon winds blow up the valley; hail and spring frost are occasional rather than constant threats.
terroir.soils: Young alluvial and colluvial soils washed off the surrounding ranges: deep sand around Cafayate, grading into stony gravel on the fans and slopes, poor in organic matter and free draining. Granite and sandstone show through in places, and the red sandstone cliffs of the Quebrada de las Conchas north of town give the landscape its colour. Phylloxera finds little purchase in the sand, so most vines stand on their own roots.
terroir.topography: The Calchaquí Valleys run north to south between Andean ranges, from Payogasta and Cachi in the north down through Molinos, Angastaco and San Carlos to Cafayate, then on into Tucumán and Catamarca. Vineyards at Cafayate sit at about 1,650 to 2,000 metres; northward the valley floor rises, and the highest plantings near Payogasta pass 3,000 metres. The steep valley sides create pockets of shade and cold air drainage that growers now map closely.
terroir.water: The Calchaquí river flows south down the valley and meets the Santa María near Cafayate, where together they become the Río de las Conchas and cut north-east through the red gorge of the Quebrada de las Conchas. Irrigation comes from these rivers and from wells, led along channels and now drip lines; without it nothing would grow.

grapes.name: Torrontés
grapes.styles: Torrontés Riojano, the finest of the three Torrontés, is the signature: roses, jasmine, white peach and citrus peel on the nose, a dry, medium bodied palate and a faint bitter finish.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Inky, dense high-altitude Malbec with black fruit, violets, dried herbs and sometimes a note of chilli pepper, and firm tannin from thick skins.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Deep and structured, often blended with Malbec; it can show a herbal, peppery edge at altitude.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.styles: A Cafayate speciality: very dark, tannic and spicy, in a valley that rivals Uruguay as the grape's South American address.

wines.note: Pale, floral and dry, with rose petal, jasmine, lychee and orange peel over brisk acidity and a slightly bitter finish. Serve cold and young; it suits empanadas salteñas, ceviche, Thai and Indian spice, and shellfish.
Deep purple, thick and concentrated, black plum and violets with a herbal or peppery edge and firm tannin; fuller than most Mendoza Malbec. Decant, and serve with grilled lamb, goat or beef.
Black fruit, liquorice and spice with big but ripe tannin; a match for barbecue, smoked meats and rich stews.
A honeyed, intensely floral dessert wine from late-picked Torrontés, sold as cosecha tardía; serve chilled with fruit tarts or blue cheese.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained either on the traditional parral, a high overhead pergola whose canopy shades fruit from the fierce sun, or on modern vertical trellises, and both are common around Cafayate. The pergola is often favoured for Torrontés, because shaded bunches keep their perfume and avoid the sunburn that turns the grape coarse and bitter. Irrigation is essential: flood channels from the rivers remain, drip lines are spreading, and water rights matter as much as land. The dry air means almost no fungal disease, so the work is managing heat, sunburn and water stress, and many old vines grow ungrafted in the sand. Harvest runs from February into April, earliest on the valley floor and latest at the top. Growers moving north up the valley to Molinos, Cachi and Payogasta are looking for colder nights; at 3,000 metres the season is short and frost a real risk.
made.winemaking: Torrontés is picked early enough to hold its acidity, pressed gently, fermented cool in stainless steel and bottled young. The risk is a bitter, phenolic finish if the skins are left in contact too long or the fruit is overripe, so careful pressing and protection from oxygen matter. Most is fully dry; late-harvest versions are sweet. Reds are given long, gentle macerations, since the thick skins yield colour and tannin easily, and are raised in French or American oak, though modern producers use less new wood and more large vats and concrete to keep the fruit forward. Blends of Malbec with Cabernet Sauvignon or Tannat are common.

law.classification: Salta's wines sell under the national framework: an Indicación Geográfica for origin, the 85 per cent rule for a named grape and a stated vintage, and no DOC. The Valles Calchaquíes name crosses provincial borders into Tucumán and Catamarca, and Cafayate, the valley's best-known town, is the origin a server most often reads. Many producers print vineyard altitude on the label, a fact rather than a legal category. Torrontés from here is nearly always Torrontés Riojano, though the label usually says only Torrontés.
tiers: Indicación Geográfica
The origin tier: Salta province or the Valles Calchaquíes; a town such as Cafayate also appears on labels as the origin.
Varietal rule
85 per cent of a named grape, and 85 per cent of a stated vintage.
labels: Altura
Vineyard altitude in metres, often printed; Cafayate fruit usually reads 1,700 metres or more.
Valles Calchaquíes
The valley system shared by Salta, Tucumán and Catamarca.
Cosecha tardía
Late harvest; in Salta usually a sweet Torrontés.

places.name: Cafayate
places.note: The town and wine centre at the south end of the valley, about 1,700 metres up, on sandy alluvial soils; the reference for Torrontés and the home of the region's oldest names, El Esteco and Etchart among them.

places.name: Yacochuya
places.note: A hamlet in the hills just above Cafayate at about 2,000 metres, with old vines on stony slopes that give some of the valley's densest Malbec.

places.name: San Carlos and Angastaco
places.note: The middle valley north of Cafayate, higher and narrower, with old vineyards of Torrontés, Malbec and Criolla among eroded sandstone formations.

places.name: Molinos
places.note: A colonial village in the upper valley where Bodega Colomé, founded in 1831, farms vineyards from about 2,300 metres upward, including pre-phylloxera vines.

places.name: Cachi and Payogasta
places.note: The northern end of the valley, where vineyards pass 3,000 metres; Colomé's Altura Máxima, at roughly 3,100 metres, is among the highest commercial vineyards in the world.

places.name: Tucumán: Amaicha and Colalao del Valle
places.note: Across the provincial border the same Calchaquí system continues, and small producers at Amaicha del Valle and Colalao del Valle make Torrontés and Malbec at roughly 1,800 to 2,000 metres.

places.name: Catamarca
places.note: The province south and west of Salta, with Santa María in the Calchaquí system and the high Fiambalá and Tinogasta valleys further west, known for Torrontés, Malbec and old Criolla.

places.name: Jujuy
places.note: The northernmost province, where a handful of growers plant in the Quebrada de Humahuaca at well over 2,000 metres; a curiosity, but the far north the exam can name.

producers.name: Bodega Colomé
producers.why: Founded in 1831 at Molinos, one of Argentina's oldest working wineries, with the Altura Máxima vineyard at roughly 3,100 metres: the altitude extreme in one bottle.

producers.name: El Esteco
producers.why: A Cafayate house founded in 1892, the valley's historic reference for Torrontés and for old-vine Malbec and Cabernet.

producers.name: Etchart
producers.why: A long-established Cafayate name for dry and late-harvest Torrontés.

producers.name: El Porvenir de Cafayate
producers.why: A Cafayate family estate known for Torrontés and for Malbec and Tannat from the valley's sandy soils.

producers.name: San Pedro de Yacochuya
producers.why: A small estate in the hills above Cafayate at about 2,000 metres, known for dense old-vine Malbec and Torrontés.

exam: Cafayate means Torrontés Riojano: floral nose, dry palate, best young and cold.
Know the geography: the Calchaquí Valleys, Cafayate at about 1,700 metres, and the upper valley, from about 2,300 metres at Molinos to over 3,000 near Payogasta.
Explain why altitude makes viticulture possible this close to the tropics: cold nights, intense ultraviolet light, thick skins.
Bodega Colomé, founded in 1831, and its Altura Máxima vineyard are the stock producer answer.
Tannat is a Cafayate speciality as well as Uruguay's grape.
traps: Cafayate itself sits around 1,700 metres; the vineyards near 3,000 metres lie up the valley near Payogasta, beyond Molinos and Cachi, so the old course note that put Cafayate near 3,000 metres was loose.
Torrontés smells sweet because of its Muscat parent but is almost always dry; only a cosecha tardía is sweet.
The Calchaquí Valleys are not only Salta's: they run on into Tucumán and Catamarca.
Salta lies near the Tropic of Capricorn, yet its wines are fresh: latitude would make it hot, altitude makes its nights cold.
Torrontés Riojano is named for La Rioja province, yet its best-known wines today come from Salta.

cards.b: Argentina's far north: Torrontés and inky Malbec from high desert valleys, Cafayate at about 1,700 metres, the upper Calchaquí above 3,000; hot days, cold nights, fierce ultraviolet light.
Roses, jasmine, peach and orange peel on the nose; dry, medium bodied and brisk, with a faint bitter finish. Drink young and cold.

cards.f: The highest vineyards of the Calchaquí Valleys
cards.b: Up the valley beyond Molinos and Cachi, near Payogasta; Colomé's Altura Máxima at roughly 3,100 metres is among the highest commercial vineyards in the world.

cards.f: Why Salta can grow wine near the tropics
cards.b: Altitude: at 1,700 to over 3,000 metres the nights are cold, the air dry and the ultraviolet strong, so grapes ripen with thick skins and keep their acidity.
Founded in 1831 at Molinos, among Argentina's oldest working wineries; pre-phylloxera vines and the Altura Máxima vineyard.
The Calchaquí and the Santa María meet near Cafayate to form the Río de las Conchas, which cuts north-east through the red sandstone Quebrada de las Conchas.
Tannat: dark, tannic and spicy; after Uruguay, Cafayate is its best-known South American home.

questions.q: Which white grape is the signature of Cafayate?
questions.exp: Torrontés Riojano is Cafayate's signature, floral on the nose and dry on the palate. Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc are grown but are not the identity, and Pedro Giménez is a bulk white of Mendoza and San Juan.

questions.q: At roughly what altitude do the vineyards around the town of Cafayate lie?
questions.exp: Cafayate's vineyards sit at about 1,650 to 2,000 metres. 3,000 metres and more is reached only further up the valley near Payogasta, and 700 to 1,000 metres is the altitude of Mendoza's lower zones.

questions.q: Which Salta winery, founded in 1831, farms the Altura Máxima vineyard?
questions.exp: Colomé, at Molinos in the upper Calchaquí Valleys, dates from 1831 and farms Altura Máxima at roughly 3,100 metres, among the highest commercial vineyards in the world.

questions.q: In which valley system does the town of Cafayate lie?
questions.exp: Cafayate lies in the south of the Valles Calchaquíes, the Calchaquí Valleys, which run north past Molinos and Cachi and south into Tucumán and Catamarca. Famatina is La Rioja's valley, Calingasta San Juan's and Uco Mendoza's.

questions.q: Apart from Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon, which red grape is a speciality of Cafayate?
questions.exp: Tannat, the grape of Madiran and Uruguay, where it was once called Harriague, ripens to dark, spicy, firmly tannic wine in Cafayate's sun, and several valley houses bottle it on its own.

questions.q: Which traditional Argentine training system is a high overhead pergola?
questions.exp: The parral is Argentina's traditional overhead pergola, and around Cafayate its canopy shades Torrontés bunches from sunburn. Guyot is cane pruning on a low wire, gobelet a free-standing bush and the lyre a divided canopy.

questions.q: Which province lies north of Salta and holds vineyards in the Quebrada de Humahuaca?
questions.exp: Jujuy is Argentina's northernmost wine province, with a few high vineyards in the Quebrada de Humahuaca. Tucumán and Catamarca lie south of Salta and share the Calchaquí system, and La Rioja is further south still.

regions.name: La Rioja
regions.summary: La Rioja is an inland province of north west Argentina, between Catamarca and San Juan, and shares nothing with Spain's Rioja beyond a name the colonists carried. Its vineyards lie mostly in the Famatina Valley around Chilecito, a hot, dry trough at roughly 900 to 1,500 metres between the Sierra de Famatina and the Sierra de Velasco. The province gave its name to Torrontés Riojano, the finest of the three Torrontés, and the grape remains its leading white: perfumed, dry and best young. Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Bonarda fill out the reds, and much of the crop passes through a large cooperative.

terroir.climate: Continental desert, hotter than the Calchaquí Valleys and close to San Juan in character. Rain is scant and falls mostly in brief summer storms, and the sun is relentless; summer days are hot, but the altitude and the clear skies bring cool nights and a wide daily swing that keeps some acidity in the grapes. Frost is a spring risk on the valley floor, hail an occasional one, and the Zonda can blow down off the ranges in late winter and spring. Humidity is so low that fungal disease is rarely a concern, which is why organic farming comes easily here.
terroir.soils: Alluvial and colluvial soils carried down from the two ranges: sand and loam on the valley floor, stony and gravelly on the fans that spread from the Famatina side. They are poor, low in organic matter and free draining, and the sand keeps phylloxera at bay, so ungrafted vines are the rule.
terroir.topography: The Famatina Valley runs north to south between the Sierra de Famatina to the west, whose summit passes 6,000 metres and carries snow much of the year, and the lower Sierra de Velasco to the east. Chilecito, Nonogasta, Anguinán and Famatina sit along its floor at roughly 900 to 1,500 metres. West again, beyond the Famatina range, the Bermejo valley around Villa Unión holds a few small, remote vineyards.
terroir.water: Snowmelt off the Sierra de Famatina feeds the streams and aquifers that irrigate the valley; the old channels still run, but wells and drip lines carry most of the water today. Water, not land, is the limit on every new planting, and a dry winter in the mountains is felt in the following harvest.

grapes.name: Torrontés
grapes.styles: Torrontés Riojano, named for the province, is the leading white: orange blossom, citrus and peach scented, dry, and at its best within a year or two of harvest.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Muscat of Alexandria, the Moscatel de Alejandría that is a parent of the Torrontés varieties, still grows here for aromatic whites.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Ripe, round and generous from the warm valley floor, fresher from the higher sites.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Grown for varietal wines and for blends with Malbec; full and ripe.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Warm, dark and spicy, suited to the heat of the valley floor.

grapes.name: Bonarda
grapes.styles: Soft, fruity reds and blending wine, often from older vines.

wines.note: The province's flagship: aromatic, dry and light to medium in body, with orange blossom, white peach and a gentle bitter edge. Serve chilled with spicy food, goat's cheese or grilled fish.
Ripe plum and blackberry, soft tannin and warmth; an easy, generous red for grilled meats and empanadas.
An everyday blend, fruit forward and lightly oaked; a value red for burgers and barbecue.

made.viticulture: The parral, the high overhead pergola, has long been the usual system in the valley, shading bunches from the fierce sun and carrying the generous crops the home market wanted; vertical trellises with drip irrigation have spread since the 1990s for wines aimed at export. Torrontés is grown widely on pergolas, where shaded fruit keeps its aroma and avoids a coarse, bitter finish. With almost no disease pressure, much of the vineyard lends itself to organic farming, and the province became an important source of organic and Fairtrade wine. The rest of the work is about water: wells, channels and drip lines decide what can be planted. Harvest begins early, often in February for white grapes, and spring frost is the main hazard on the valley floor.
made.winemaking: Most wine is made in large modern cellars, much of it by the cooperative at Chilecito, which handles grapes from many small growers. Torrontés is pressed gently, fermented cool in stainless steel and bottled young to keep its perfume; the skill lies in avoiding the phenolic bitterness the grape develops with too much skin contact or ripeness. Reds are fermented warm for colour, with oak used sparingly in the value tiers and more generously in reserve wines. Blending across the valley is common for the everyday ranges, and some wine leaves the province in bulk.

law.classification: La Rioja works under the national framework: an Indicación Geográfica for origin, the 85 per cent rule for a named grape and a stated vintage, and no DOC that a server is likely to meet. The Valle de Famatina is the origin most fine labels name, and many bottles simply say La Rioja. Organic and Fairtrade certifications appear often on export labels. The province's name on a bottle never means Spanish Rioja: Argentine La Rioja carries no ageing ladder and no Tempranillo tradition.

The province of La Rioja, or a valley within it such as Famatina.
Varietal rule
85 per cent of a named grape; 85 per cent of a stated vintage.
labels: Torrontés Riojano
The grape's full name, after the province; usually written only Torrontés.
Valle de Famatina
The valley around Chilecito, the province's main wine area.

A certification common on the cooperative's export wines; it describes trade, not quality.

places.name: Valle de Famatina
places.note: The heart of the province's wine, a north to south valley between the Sierra de Famatina and the Sierra de Velasco, irrigated by snowmelt; Torrontés Riojano leads, with Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.

places.name: Chilecito
places.note: The valley's main town, about 1,100 metres up, seat of the large cooperative that gathers grapes from many small growers, and of an early twentieth-century cable way that once brought ore down from the Famatina mines.

places.name: Nonogasta
places.note: A district south of Chilecito on the valley floor, warm and low, with old pergola vineyards of Torrontés and Malbec.

places.name: Famatina
places.note: The town at the valley's northern end, higher and cooler, beneath the snow-capped range that gives the valley its name.

places.name: Chañarmuyo
places.note: A high site in the north of the valley at about 1,700 metres, where a modern estate grows Torrontés, Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon on stony slopes.

places.name: Valle del Bermejo
places.note: West of the Famatina range around Villa Unión, a more remote valley with a small number of vineyards on stony ground beneath red sandstone cliffs; a frontier name rather than a reference, and a sign that growers are looking for altitude here as they are in Salta.

producers.name: La Riojana
producers.why: The large Chilecito cooperative of many small growers, the province's biggest producer and one of the world's leading sources of Fairtrade wine.

producers.name: Bodega Chañarmuyo
producers.why: A modern estate at about 1,700 metres in the north of the Famatina Valley, showing what altitude does for the province's Torrontés and Malbec.

exam: La Rioja gave its name to Torrontés Riojano, the finest and most perfumed of the three Torrontés.
The Famatina Valley around Chilecito is the province's wine heart, between the Sierra de Famatina and the Sierra de Velasco.
Know where La Rioja sits: north of San Juan, south of Catamarca, grouped by Wines of Argentina with San Juan and Mendoza in Cuyo.
Torrontés Riojano's parents are Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, the Listán Prieto of the missions.
The cooperative tradition, Fairtrade and organic wine are the province's trade story.
traps: La Rioja, Argentina, is not Rioja, Spain: no Tempranillo tradition, no ageing tiers, a different hemisphere.
Torrontés Riojano is named for this province, but the grape's best-known wines today come from Cafayate in Salta.
Argentine Torrontés has no link to the Torrontés of Galicia's Ribeiro, a different grape that shares the name.
The valley floor is hot; the freshness comes from altitude and cool nights, not from latitude.

cards.b: A hot, dry province between Catamarca and San Juan; the Famatina Valley around Chilecito; Torrontés Riojano named for it, with Malbec and Cabernet. Not Spain's Rioja.
Muscat of Alexandria crossed naturally with Criolla Chica, the mission grape Spain calls Listán Prieto. Torrontés Sanjuanino has the same parents.
The Sierra de Famatina to the west, above 6,000 metres and snow capped, and the lower Sierra de Velasco to the east.
The Famatina Valley's main town, about 1,100 metres up, home of the large La Riojana cooperative.
Many small growers, a large cooperative and a leading role in Fairtrade and organic wine, helped by dry air that keeps disease away.

cards.f: La Rioja, Argentina, against Rioja, Spain
cards.b: Argentine province: Torrontés and Malbec, IG and the 85 per cent rule. Spanish DOCa: Tempranillo and the Crianza to Gran Reserva ageing ladder. Same name, nothing else shared.

cards.f: Why Torrontés is grown on pergolas here
cards.b: The overhead parral shades bunches from fierce sun, keeping aroma and acidity and avoiding the coarse, bitter finish of sunburnt fruit.

questions.q: Which grape is La Rioja's leading white?
questions.exp: Torrontés Riojano, named for the province, is La Rioja's leading white, perfumed yet dry. Moscatel de Alejandría grows here in small amounts, Pedro Giménez is the bulk white of Mendoza and San Juan, and Chardonnay is Mendoza's leading quality white.

questions.q: Which grape is one parent of Torrontés Riojano?
questions.exp: DNA profiling shows Torrontés Riojano is a natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, the Listán Prieto of the Spanish missions; its orange blossom perfume comes from that Muscat, not from the small-berried Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains.

questions.q: Which valley around Chilecito is La Rioja's main wine area?
questions.exp: The Famatina Valley runs between the Sierra de Famatina and the Sierra de Velasco, with Chilecito its main town; it grows most of the province's Torrontés Riojano and Malbec.

questions.q: At roughly what altitude do La Rioja's main vineyards lie?
questions.exp: La Rioja's main vineyards lie on a hot valley floor at roughly 900 to 1,500 metres, where clear skies bring cool nights. 200 to 400 metres is Patagonia's range, and 2,000 metres and more belongs to Salta's Calchaquí Valleys.

questions.q: Which wine province lies between La Rioja and Mendoza?
questions.exp: San Juan lies between La Rioja and Mendoza. Catamarca and Salta are north of La Rioja, and Neuquén is in northern Patagonia, south of Mendoza.

questions.q: What lets La Rioja's growers farm organically with ease?
questions.exp: The air is so dry that fungal disease rarely takes hold, so growers need few sprays and organic farming comes easily. La Rioja's summers are hot, its soils alluvial, and it lies far from any sea.

questions.q: Under what name does Argentina grow the Listán Prieto that is a parent of Torrontés?
questions.exp: Criolla Chica is Argentina's name for Listán Prieto, the mission grape that Chile calls País and California Mission; crossed with Muscat of Alexandria it gave Torrontés Riojano.

regions.name: San Juan
regions.summary: San Juan, north of Mendoza, is second only to Mendoza in Argentine vineyard and volume, and the hottest and driest of the major provinces. Most vines grow in the Tulum Valley around the city of San Juan at about 600 to 700 metres, where heat, sun and around a hundred millimetres of rain a year make big, ripe wines, alongside much of the country's table grapes, raisins and grape concentrate. Syrah is the grape the province made its name with, warm and spicy; Bonarda, Malbec and Cabernet follow. The quality frontier lies higher and to the west, in the Zonda, Ullum, Pedernal and Calingasta valleys, where altitude restores freshness.

terroir.climate: Hot continental desert. The Tulum Valley receives around 100 millimetres of rain a year or less, summers are hot and the sun almost unbroken, and the Zonda, which takes its name from a valley in this province, can blow hot and dry off the Andes in late winter and spring. Nights cool sharply, but the valley floor is one of the warmest places in Argentine viticulture. The western valleys at 1,300 to 1,600 metres, Pedernal and Calingasta, are markedly cooler, with frost a real spring risk.
terroir.soils: On the Tulum floor, deep alluvial soils of sand, silt and clay laid down by the San Juan river, fertile enough to carry large crops. Towards the foothills and in the western valleys the ground turns stony and poor: gravel, cobbles and boulders on alluvial fans, free draining and low in organic matter, which growers prize for concentration and structure.
terroir.topography: The Tulum Valley is a broad basin around the city of San Juan at roughly 600 to 700 metres, with the Ullum and Zonda valleys tucked against the precordillera just west of it at about 750 to 900 metres. South west lies the Pedernal Valley at around 1,350 metres, and further west, behind the precordillera, the long Calingasta Valley around Barreal and Calingasta at 1,400 metres and more, facing the high Andes. To the north the Jáchal and Iglesia valleys carry scattered vineyards.
terroir.water: The San Juan river, fed by Andean snow, irrigates the Tulum Valley through the Ullum reservoir and a network of canals; in the west the Los Patos river waters the Calingasta Valley. Water is scarcer than in Mendoza, and dry winters in the mountains test the whole system.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The province's calling card since the 1990s: ripe blackberry, plum, pepper and smoked meat, softer and warmer than Rhône Syrah, finer from Pedernal and Calingasta.

grapes.name: Bonarda
grapes.styles: Juicy, dark and low in tannin, for fruity reds and blending; widely planted on the valley floor.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Ripe and full on the Tulum floor, taut and floral from Pedernal at altitude.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripe, round Cabernet, and blends with Syrah and Malbec.

grapes.name: Torrontés
grapes.styles: Torrontés Sanjuanino, named for the province, is less perfumed than Riojano; Torrontés Riojano is also grown.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Small plantings in the warm Tulum Valley give rich, apricot-scented whites.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Fresh, citrus and stony Chardonnay from the high Calingasta and Pedernal valleys.

grapes.name: Pedro Giménez
grapes.styles: A high-yielding white for bulk wine, must and concentrate; not Spain's Pedro Ximénez.

wines.note: Full and ripe: blackberry, plum, black pepper and a smoky note, round tannin and warmth; a red for barbecue, sausages and smoked brisket.
High-altitude Malbec of violet, dark cherry and graphite with fresh acidity and fine tannin; serve with lamb or a sirloin steak.
Soft, juicy and purple, cherry and plum with little tannin; drink young and slightly cool with pizza, pasta or empanadas.
Taut and citrus scented with a stony edge from the high western vineyards; with fish, chicken or a crab salad.

made.viticulture: The Tulum Valley was planted for volume, and the parral, the high pergola, still covers much of it, carrying heavy crops of Bonarda, Cereza, Criolla Grande, Pedro Giménez and table grapes and shading the bunches from the heat. Quality estates replanted on vertical trellises with drip irrigation from the 1990s, chose cooler pockets and picked earlier to keep acidity. The newer western valleys are planted on stony fans at 1,300 metres and above, with dense trellised rows, careful water budgets and frost protection. The hazards are heat, the Zonda at flowering, occasional hail and, in the high valleys, spring frost. Phylloxera is present, but much of the vineyard still grows ungrafted in sand. Harvest on the Tulum floor starts early, in February for most grapes, and weeks later in Pedernal and Calingasta.
made.winemaking: The province makes three kinds of product: everyday wine, the grape must and concentrate sold as a sweetener for juices and soft drinks, and fine wine. Fine Syrah and Malbec are cold soaked and fermented in stainless steel or concrete, then aged in French and American oak; producers on the Tulum floor have moved towards earlier picking and less new wood to keep the fruit lively. Bonarda is often made without oak for freshness, and whites are fermented cool to hold their aroma against the heat. Some houses blend Tulum fruit for body with Pedernal or Calingasta fruit for acidity, a corte across altitudes.

law.classification: San Juan works under the national framework: an Indicación Geográfica for origin, 85 per cent for a named grape and a stated vintage, and no DOC. Most bottles name San Juan or the Tulum Valley; the higher valleys, Zonda, Ullum, Pedernal and Calingasta, appear on labels as the origins of the finer wines, several of them registered as IGs. Torrontés Sanjuanino carries the province's name, but on a label it is simply Torrontés.

San Juan province, or a valley within it such as Tulum, Pedernal or Calingasta.
Varietal rule
85 per cent of a named grape and of a stated vintage.
labels: Valle de Tulum
The main valley around the city of San Juan; warm, low and large scale.
Valle de Pedernal
The high south-western valley at about 1,350 metres; the province's fine-wine frontier.
Torrontés Sanjuanino
The province's own Torrontés, less perfumed than Riojano; labelled simply Torrontés.

places.name: Valle de Tulum
places.note: The broad basin around the city of San Juan, 600 to 700 metres up, warm and irrigated from the San Juan river; most of the province's wine, table grapes and raisins come from here.

places.name: Valle del Zonda
places.note: A small valley just west of the city against the precordillera, a little higher and cooler than Tulum; its name is the hot wind's.

places.name: Valle de Ullum
places.note: North west of the city around the Ullum reservoir, about 800 metres up on stony ground, giving fresher reds than the valley floor.

places.name: Valle de Pedernal
places.note: A high valley in the south west at about 1,350 metres, cool at night, with stony soils; the reference for San Juan's finer Malbec, Syrah and Chardonnay.

places.name: Valle de Calingasta
places.note: West behind the precordillera, a long valley at 1,400 metres and more beneath the high Andes, watered by the Los Patos river; cool, remote and home to old Criolla vines as well as new plantings.

places.name: Barreal
places.note: The southern town of the Calingasta Valley, at about 1,600 metres, where small producers work old pergola vines of Criolla and new plantings of Malbec.

places.name: Jáchal and Iglesia
places.note: Northern valleys with scattered, high vineyards; small, traditional and rarely seen on export lists.

producers.name: Graffigna
producers.why: Founded in San Juan in 1870, the province's best-known historic house.

producers.name: Finca Las Moras
producers.why: A large Tulum Valley producer that carried San Juan Syrah onto export lists.

producers.name: Callia
producers.why: A Tulum Valley estate built around Syrah, a value reference for the province's warm style.

producers.name: Pyros
producers.why: A Pedernal Valley estate at about 1,400 metres, showing what altitude does for San Juan Malbec and Syrah.

producers.name: Cara Sur
producers.why: A small Barreal project bottling old pergola Criolla and other heritage grapes from the Calingasta Valley.

exam: San Juan is Argentina's second wine province, north of Mendoza, hotter and drier.
Syrah is the grape the province is known for; Bonarda and Malbec follow.
The Tulum Valley is the volume heart; Pedernal and Calingasta are the high, cool frontier.
The Zonda wind takes its name from San Juan's Zonda valley.
San Juan gives its name to Torrontés Sanjuanino, the less aromatic cousin of Riojano.
Much of the crop becomes table grapes, raisins and grape concentrate rather than wine.
traps: San Juan Syrah is warm and ripe; do not describe it like Northern Rhône Syrah from granite slopes.
Torrontés Sanjuanino shares Riojano's parents yet is a different, less perfumed variety.
San Juan lies north of Mendoza, between it and La Rioja, not south of it.
Pedro Giménez, widely planted here, is not Spain's Pedro Ximénez.
Not every San Juan wine is hot climate: Pedernal and Calingasta sit at 1,300 metres and above and can be as fresh as the Uco Valley.

cards.b: Argentina's second wine province, north of Mendoza: hot, dry Tulum Valley Syrah, Bonarda and Malbec, table grapes and concentrate; high, cool Pedernal and Calingasta for finer wine.
Syrah: ripe blackberry, plum, pepper and smoke from the Tulum Valley, fresher and finer from Pedernal.

cards.f: Where the Zonda gets its name
cards.b: The hot, dry Andean foehn of western Argentina is named for the Zonda valley just west of San Juan city.
Pedernal, about 1,350 metres, in the south west; Calingasta, 1,400 metres and more around Barreal, behind the precordillera. Cool nights, stony soils, fresher wines.
Around 100 millimetres a year or less, among the driest of Argentine wine regions; the San Juan river and the Ullum reservoir make the valley farmable.
The second of the three Torrontés, named for San Juan; the same parents as Riojano, Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, but less perfumed.
San Juan's best-known historic house, founded in 1870.

questions.q: Which red grape is San Juan best known for?
questions.exp: Syrah made San Juan's reputation from the 1990s, ripe and spicy from the Tulum Valley. Tannat is Cafayate's speciality, Pinot Noir Patagonia's and Cabernet Franc a rising grape of the Uco Valley.

questions.q: Which valley around San Juan city grows most of the province's grapes?
questions.exp: The Tulum Valley, a broad basin at 600 to 700 metres irrigated from the San Juan river, carries most of the province's wine grapes, table grapes and raisins.

questions.q: Which valley of western San Juan, behind the precordillera, holds the town of Barreal?
questions.exp: The Calingasta Valley lies at 1,400 metres and more beneath the high Andes, watered by the Los Patos river; Barreal, its southern town, keeps old pergola Criolla beside new plantings of Malbec.

questions.q: At roughly what altitude does San Juan's Pedernal Valley lie?
questions.exp: Pedernal sits at about 1,350 metres in the south west of the province, far above the Tulum Valley's 600 to 700 metres; 3,000 metres belongs to Salta's upper Calchaquí and 300 metres to Patagonia.

questions.q: By vineyard area, where does San Juan rank among Argentina's wine provinces?
questions.exp: San Juan is second only to Mendoza in vineyard and volume, and much of its crop becomes table grapes, raisins and grape concentrate as well as wine.

questions.q: Roughly how much rain does the city of San Juan receive in a year?
questions.exp: San Juan receives around 100 millimetres a year or less, among the driest of Argentina's wine regions, so snowmelt from the San Juan river, stored behind the Ullum dam, waters the vines. Mendoza city sees about 200.

questions.q: Which wine province lies directly south of San Juan?
questions.exp: Mendoza lies directly south of San Juan. La Rioja is to the north with Catamarca beyond it, while Neuquén lies further south, past Mendoza, in northern Patagonia.

regions.name: Mendoza (Uco, Luján de Cuyo)
regions.summary: Mendoza is Argentine wine: the province holds most of the country's vineyard and nearly all of its famous names. It lies on the eastern foot of the Andes in a rain shadow so complete that every vine is irrigated with snowmelt. Malbec is the grape, and two addresses carry the exam: Luján de Cuyo, the historic first zone just south of Mendoza city at 900 to 1,100 metres, home of the country's first DOC and of plush, classic Malbec; and the Uco Valley, higher at 900 to over 1,500 metres, whose stony fans give tauter, more floral Malbec and fine Chardonnay. Maipú, the East and San Rafael complete the picture.

terroir.climate: High continental desert. Mendoza city receives around 200 millimetres of rain a year, most of it in summer storms that bring the province's great hazard, hail. Days are hot and sunny, nights cold, and the daily swing often passes fifteen degrees. Altitude sets the temperature: the East and San Rafael are warm, Luján de Cuyo and Maipú moderate, the Uco Valley cool, with spring frost a real risk there. The Zonda, a hot, dry foehn off the Andes, strikes mostly in late winter and spring and can damage budburst and flowering.
terroir.soils: Alluvial throughout, laid down by the rivers that leave the Andes. The first zone mixes sand, silt and clay with gravel near the Mendoza river, deeper and loamier at Agrelo, stonier at Perdriel and Barrancas. The Uco Valley is a sequence of alluvial fans: rounded stones and gravel under thin sandy topsoil, often coated with calcium carbonate, and patches of genuinely calcareous ground at Gualtallary and Paraje Altamira. The East is deep, fertile sand and silt. Most soils are poor in organic matter and free draining, and sand lets most vines grow ungrafted.
terroir.topography: The vineyards spread east from the Andes in steps. Mendoza city sits at about 750 metres; Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, the first zone, lie just south at 750 to 1,100 metres. The Uco Valley, an hour south west, is a high trough between the Cordón del Plata and the main Andes to the west and low hills to the east, planted from about 900 metres to over 1,500 in Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos. The East is a flat plain at 600 to 750 metres; San Rafael and General Alvear in the south lie at roughly 450 to 800.
terroir.water: Four Andean rivers make the province farmable: the Mendoza, which waters Luján de Cuyo, Maipú and the north; the Tunuyán, which crosses the Uco Valley and then feeds the East; and the Diamante and Atuel in the south around San Rafael. Dams such as Potrerillos store the snowmelt, and the acequias begun by the Huarpe people still line the streets of Mendoza city.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: The national grape: violet, black plum and cocoa with plush tannin from Luján de Cuyo, more floral and herbal, with a chalky grip, from the Uco Valley's high fans.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Ripe cassis and herb, often with Malbec in a corte; fine from Agrelo and the old vines of Maipú.

grapes.name: Bonarda
grapes.styles: The province's second red, planted widely in the East for juicy, soft reds and blends.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: The rising grape of the Uco Valley, herbal and floral, made on its own and in blends.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The leading quality white, taut and saline from Gualtallary, rounder from Agrelo, and the base of traditional-method sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Grown high in the Uco Valley for still wine and for sparkling base.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: Old vines in the Uco Valley and San Rafael, rediscovered for textured, waxy whites.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Old vines survive in parts of the province, the south among them, for fresh, lightly honeyed whites.

wines.note: The classic: dark plum, blackberry, violet and mocha, full body and velvet tannin, often with French oak. Serve slightly below room temperature with steak, asado and short rib.
Brighter and tauter: red and black cherry, violets, dried herbs and a chalky, gravelly grip with fresh acidity; decant and pour with lamb, duck or mushrooms.
The flagship blend of the great houses, structured and long lived, Malbec's perfume over Cabernet's frame; for rib of beef and aged steaks.
Saline, citrus and stony, with restrained oak and firm acidity; with fish, crab and poultry in butter sauces.
Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from high Uco vineyards, crisp and creamy, made on a large scale since Chandon arrived in 1959; an aperitif and a match for fried oysters.
Soft, purple and juicy with cherry and plum; an everyday red for pizza and pasta.

made.viticulture: Irrigation defines the work. Water rights, flood channels and, more and more, drip lines decide what can be planted, and the snowpack that fills the dams is watched every winter. The traditional parral, a high pergola, still covers old vineyards in the first zone and much of the East, carrying big crops; quality plantings since the 1990s are on vertical trellises at higher density. Black or white hail nets stretch over the best rows, because a summer storm can strip a vineyard in minutes. In the Uco Valley frost is the second threat, met with wind machines, sprinklers and site choice. Most vines grow on their own roots, and old Malbec in Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, propagated by massal selection, became the source material for the new high plantings. Harvest runs from February in the East to late April in the Uco Valley, and over the 2010s the move uphill and towards earlier picking reshaped the style.
made.winemaking: The Mendoza Malbec that won export markets in the 2000s was ripe, extracted and raised in new French oak. The style has since turned: earlier picking, gentler extraction, whole bunches in some cellars, and fermentation and ageing in concrete tanks, concrete eggs and large casks rather than new barriques. Single-site bottlings from soil-mapped districts are the fashion at the top, while blends across zones, Malbec with Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc or Petit Verdot, remain the grand wines of the great houses. Chardonnay is barrel fermented with less new wood than before. Sparkling wine became a Mendoza industry after Moët & Chandon founded Bodegas Chandon in 1959, its first venture outside France. In the East, large cellars make everyday wine, bulk wine and grape concentrate.

law.classification: Mendoza carries both of the DOCs a server meets. Luján de Cuyo, recognised in 1989, was the first, built around Malbec; San Rafael, in the south, is the second. Neither appears on many labels. The working system is the Indicación Geográfica, which nests from the province through the Uco Valley and the departments down to districts, most of them drawn on alluvial fans and soil surveys rather than political lines: Paraje Altamira, recognised in 2013, Los Chacayes in 2017, San Pablo in 2019, and El Peral, by a resolution numbered 1/2022 and gazetted in January 2023. Wines of Argentina's division into the first zone, the Uco Valley, the East, the North and the South describes the province without being law. A named grape or vintage must reach 85 per cent.
tiers: DOC Luján de Cuyo
The first DOC, of 1989, for Malbec-based wine from the department of Luján de Cuyo; rarely printed.
DOC San Rafael
The second DOC, in southern Mendoza; rarely printed.
IG Mendoza
The province, the broadest origin on most bottles.
IG Valle de Uco
The high valley of Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos.
Departments
Names such as Luján de Cuyo, Maipú, Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos serve as origins within the province.
Uco Valley district IGs
Smaller IGs inside the valley, most drawn by soil survey: Paraje Altamira (2013), Los Chacayes (2017), San Pablo (2019), El Peral (gazetted 2023).
labels: Primera Zona
The first zone: Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, the historic heart; a trade term.
Valle de Uco
The Uco Valley; the high frontier.
Paraje
A named district; Paraje Altamira is an IG, the word itself is not.
Finca
Estate or single vineyard; no legal rank.
Corte
A blend; Malbec with Cabernet Sauvignon is the classic.

places.name: Primera Zona
places.note: The first zone just south of Mendoza city along the Mendoza river, 750 to 1,100 metres up: the historic heart of fine wine, old ungrafted Malbec and the seat of the great houses.

places.name: Luján de Cuyo
places.note: The department of the first DOC, at 900 to 1,100 metres, where classic, plush Malbec grows on alluvial sand, clay and gravel; Catena Zapata, Chandon and Terrazas de los Andes have cellars here.

places.name: Agrelo
places.note: The southern, higher part of Luján de Cuyo, with deeper, clay-rich soils, cool nights and many modern estates; full, structured Malbec and Cabernet.

places.name: Perdriel
places.note: Beside the Mendoza river, stony and well drained, giving firm, concentrated Malbec; Terrazas de los Andes has its cellar here.

places.name: Vistalba and Las Compuertas
places.note: Western districts of the first zone near the river, around 1,000 to 1,100 metres, with old vineyards prized for perfumed Malbec.

places.name: Maipú
places.note: Lower and warmer, at 750 to 950 metres east of Luján, with old vines and a name for Cabernet Sauvignon as well as Malbec; Lunlunta and Barrancas, on stony ground beside the Mendoza river, are the quality districts, and Trapiche is an old resident.

places.name: Lunlunta
places.note: Old Malbec on the river terraces, including Catena Zapata's Angélica vineyard.

places.name: Valle de Uco
places.note: An hour south west of the city, the high valley of three departments, Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos, planted from about 900 to over 1,500 metres on alluvial fans beneath the Andes: cooler, tauter wines, and the source of the modern style.

places.name: Tupungato
places.note: The northern department and the highest overall, with Gualtallary and El Peral; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling base as well as Malbec.

places.name: Gualtallary
places.note: The northern district of Tupungato, from about 1,200 to over 1,500 metres, with calcareous patches; Catena Zapata's Adrianna vineyard, planted in 1992 at about 1,450 metres, made its name, and its own IG has long been sought.

places.name: El Peral
places.note: A cool district of Tupungato, recognised as an IG at the request of Chandon, the sparkling wine house, by a resolution gazetted in January 2023.

places.name: Tunuyán
places.note: The middle department, with Vista Flores, Los Chacayes and San Pablo; stony fans and some of the valley's highest plantings.

places.name: Los Chacayes
places.note: A wild, boulder-strewn fan above 1,000 metres beneath the Andes, an IG since 2017; dense, firmly tannic Malbec.

places.name: San Pablo
places.note: One of the valley's highest districts, an IG since 2019, cold at night and frost prone; fresh Malbec, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Vista Flores
places.note: Home of Clos de los Siete, a late 1990s venture by Bordeaux investors, and of many estates on sandy, stony ground.

places.name: San Carlos
places.note: The southern department, with the old vines of La Consulta, Paraje Altamira and the cold, frost-prone El Cepillo.

places.name: Paraje Altamira
places.note: The first of the Uco Valley's IGs drawn by soil survey, recognised in 2013, on the Tunuyán river's fan at about 1,000 to 1,200 metres; stones coated with calcium carbonate give chalk-textured, tense Malbec, Zuccardi's Piedra Infinita the reference.

places.name: La Consulta
places.note: An old farming town with some of the Uco Valley's oldest Malbec and Sémillon vines.

places.name: East Mendoza
places.note: The flat eastern plain of San Martín, Junín, Rivadavia and Santa Rosa at 600 to 750 metres, irrigated from the lower Mendoza and Tunuyán rivers: the province's volume, from Bonarda, Criolla, Cereza and Pedro Giménez, and much of its bulk wine and concentrate.

places.name: North Mendoza
places.note: The low, hot country around Lavalle and Las Heras, north and east of the city, planted for volume and for white grapes.

places.name: San Rafael
places.note: The southern oasis around San Rafael and General Alvear, 450 to 800 metres up, watered by the Diamante and Atuel rivers; Argentina's second DOC, with Malbec, Cabernet, Bonarda and some old white vines, and more hail than the north.

producers.name: Catena Zapata
producers.why: Founded by Nicola Catena in 1902, the house that led the move to altitude with the Adrianna vineyard and set the benchmark for Argentine Malbec and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Catena Zapata Adrianna Vineyard
producers.why: Planted at Gualtallary in 1992 at about 1,450 metres; its separately bottled parcels are the classic lesson in Uco altitude and soil.

producers.name: Familia Zuccardi
producers.why: Founded in 1963 and now centred on the Piedra Infinita winery in Paraje Altamira: concrete, little new oak, site over ripeness.

producers.name: Achaval-Ferrer
producers.why: Founded in 1998, an early champion of single-vineyard Malbec, bottling Finca Altamira and Finca Bella Vista apart.

producers.name: Terrazas de los Andes
producers.why: Founded by Moët Hennessy in Mendoza in 1996 on the idea of matching each grape to its altitude band, and the Argentine partner in Cheval des Andes.

producers.name: Cheval des Andes
producers.why: The joint venture with Château Cheval Blanc, first vintage 1999, a blend of Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec usually leading; Argentina's entry in the French joint-venture set with Almaviva and Opus One.

producers.name: Bodegas Chandon
producers.why: Founded by Moët & Chandon in 1959, its first winery outside France, and the reason Mendoza makes traditional-method sparkling wine on a large scale.

producers.name: Bodega Norton
producers.why: Founded in 1895 by the English engineer Edmund James Palmer Norton, one of the historic houses of Luján de Cuyo.

producers.name: Trapiche
producers.why: Founded in 1883 in Mendoza, with its historic cellar in Maipú, one of Argentina's oldest and largest houses, with a long series of single-vineyard Malbecs.

producers.name: Clos de los Siete
producers.why: A Vista Flores project of Bordeaux investors from the late 1990s, whose Malbec-led blend introduced the Uco Valley to many lists.

producers.name: Bodegas Bianchi
producers.why: Founded in San Rafael in 1928, the historic house of southern Mendoza, for still and sparkling wine.

exam: Malbec is Mendoza: Luján de Cuyo for classic, plush Malbec, the Uco Valley for high, taut, floral Malbec.
Luján de Cuyo took Argentina's first DOC in 1989; San Rafael holds the second.
The Uco Valley's three departments are Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos; Gualtallary, Paraje Altamira and Los Chacayes are the districts to name.
Explain snowmelt irrigation, hail nets, the Zonda and spring frost in the Uco Valley.
Know the producer links: Catena Zapata and Adrianna, Zuccardi and Paraje Altamira, Cheval des Andes and Cheval Blanc, Chandon since 1959.
Know the rivers: the Mendoza feeds the first zone, the Tunuyán the Uco Valley and the East, the Diamante and Atuel San Rafael.
traps: The Uco Valley sits higher and cooler than Luján de Cuyo; its Malbec is tauter and more floral, not bigger.

Gualtallary is a district of Tupungato in the Uco Valley; the Codex's producer note that calls it a GI runs ahead of the register, since no IG resolution for it could be found when this article was written.
Paraje Altamira is in San Carlos in the Uco Valley, not in Luján de Cuyo.
Maipú is lower and warmer than Luján de Cuyo, and its old vines are known for Cabernet Sauvignon as well as Malbec.
The calcareous ground of the Uco Valley is patchy, inside alluvial fans, not a continuous limestone bed like Burgundy's.
Cheval des Andes is usually Malbec led with Cabernet Sauvignon, not a Cabernet Franc and Merlot blend in Cheval Blanc's image.
San Rafael in Mendoza is not the San Rafael of Chile's Maule.

cards.b: Most of Argentina's vineyard, on the eastern foot of the Andes and irrigated by snowmelt: Malbec, plush from Luján de Cuyo, taut and floral from the high Uco Valley.

cards.f: Luján de Cuyo against the Uco Valley
cards.b: Luján: first zone, 900 to 1,100 metres, first DOC (1989), classic plush Malbec. Uco: 900 to over 1,500 metres, alluvial fans, cooler, tauter, more floral Malbec and fine Chardonnay.
Tupungato (north: Gualtallary, El Peral), Tunuyán (middle: Los Chacayes, Vista Flores, San Pablo), San Carlos (south: Paraje Altamira, La Consulta, El Cepillo).

cards.f: Mendoza's rivers and what they water
cards.b: The Mendoza: Luján de Cuyo, Maipú and the north. The Tunuyán: the Uco Valley, then the East. The Diamante and Atuel: San Rafael.
An IG since 2013, drawn by soil survey, in San Carlos; stones coated with calcium carbonate on the Tunuyán river's fan; chalky, tense Malbec.
Summer hail, met with nets; the Zonda, a hot, dry Andean wind of late winter and spring; and spring frost in the high Uco Valley.
Founded by Moët & Chandon in 1959, its first winery outside France; traditional-method sparkling wine from high Uco Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
Luján de Cuyo (1989, built around Malbec) and San Rafael in the south. Both rarely appear on labels; the IG is the working tier.

cards.f: Cheval des Andes in one line
cards.b: Château Cheval Blanc with Terrazas de los Andes, first vintage 1999; Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec usually leading.

questions.q: Which Mendoza department holds Argentina's first DOC?
questions.exp: Luján de Cuyo was recognised as a DOC in 1989 for its Malbec. Maipú is the lower, warmer neighbour in the first zone, Tupungato an Uco Valley department and General Alvear lies in the south beside San Rafael.

questions.q: In which Mendoza department does Paraje Altamira lie?
questions.exp: Paraje Altamira lies in San Carlos, the Uco Valley's southern department, on the Tunuyán river's fan, and became an IG in 2013. Tupungato and Tunuyán are the valley's other departments, and Luján de Cuyo is the first zone south of the city.

questions.q: Which Uco Valley department holds the district of Gualtallary?
questions.exp: Gualtallary lies in the north of Tupungato, the highest of the Uco Valley's three departments; Catena Zapata planted its Adrianna vineyard there at about 1,450 metres in 1992.

questions.q: Which river irrigates the Uco Valley?
questions.exp: The Tunuyán crosses the Uco Valley before watering the East. The Mendoza river feeds Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, and the Diamante and Atuel serve San Rafael in the south.

questions.q: Which Mendoza zone holds Argentina's second DOC?
questions.exp: San Rafael, the southern oasis watered by the Diamante and Atuel rivers, holds the second DOC after Luján de Cuyo. Maipú and Tupungato are department origins without DOC status, and Paraje Altamira is an IG.

questions.q: Which Bordeaux estate partners Terrazas de los Andes in Cheval des Andes?
questions.exp: Cheval des Andes joins the Saint-Émilion estate Château Cheval Blanc with Terrazas de los Andes; the first vintage was 1999, a blend of Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon.

questions.q: Which measure protects Mendoza's best vineyards from summer hail?
questions.exp: Black or white hail nets stretched over the rows protect the fruit from summer hailstorms. Wind machines, sprinklers and smudge pots are frost defences, used in the Uco Valley in spring.

questions.q: Which department joins Luján de Cuyo in Mendoza's Primera Zona?
questions.exp: Maipú, lower and warmer than Luján at 750 to 950 metres and known for old-vine Cabernet Sauvignon as well as Malbec, completes the first zone. Tupungato and San Carlos are Uco Valley departments, and Lavalle lies in the hot north.

regions.name: Patagonia (Río Negro/Neuquén)
regions.summary: Patagonia is Argentina's cool south, though its vineyards lie in the north of that vast region, in the irrigated river valleys of Río Negro and Neuquén around 38 to 39 degrees south. Unlike the Andean north, the vineyards are low, at roughly 200 to 400 metres: the cooling comes from latitude, cold nights, an early autumn and an almost constant westerly wind. Pinot Noir is the grape the region is praised for, pale, spicy and fresh, and Malbec here is red fruited and lifted. The Alto Valle del Río Negro is the historic heart and San Patricio del Chañar in Neuquén the modern one; La Pampa and Chubut add outposts.

terroir.climate: Continental desert, with under 200 millimetres of rain and very low humidity. Summer days are warm and long, for the latitude gives more hours of light than Mendoza in high summer, but nights are cold and the season ends earlier, with frost possible at both ends. The wind, strong and westerly, blows for much of the year: it keeps disease away, thickens skins and slows ripening. Hail is rarer than in Mendoza. The result is a long, cool finish to ripening that holds acidity and keeps alcohol in check.
terroir.soils: River terraces of alluvial sand and gravel over clay, laid down by the Neuquén, the Limay and the Negro, with stonier ground towards the edges of the valleys. Above the valleys rise the bardas, the steep edges of the arid plateau, and the ground at their foot is often the best drained. The soils are poor in organic matter except where generations of orchards have enriched them.
terroir.topography: The Neuquén and Limay rivers meet at the city of Neuquén to form the Río Negro, which flows east across the Patagonian plateau in a green ribbon of orchards and vineyards: the Alto Valle first, then the Valle Medio further downstream. San Patricio del Chañar lies on a plateau north west of Neuquén city above the Neuquén river. Elevations are low, roughly 200 to 400 metres, and the land is flat to gently sloping beneath the bardas.
terroir.water: Everything depends on the rivers. Canals built in the early twentieth century turned the Alto Valle into Argentina's apple and pear orchard, with vineyards among the fruit; the vineyards of San Patricio del Chañar, on plateau land watered from the Neuquén river, are far younger, planted from the late 1990s. Lines of poplars break the wind along the canals.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The region's pride: pale, high toned and spicy, rosehip, red cherry and earth, from old own-rooted vines in Río Negro and newer plantings in Neuquén.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Red fruited, fresher and less dense than Mendoza's, with firm acidity and a floral lift.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Plummy and fresh in Neuquén and Río Negro, made on its own and in blends.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Crisp, citrus and herb-scented whites from the cooler sites.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: Old vines in the Alto Valle give waxy, long-lived whites.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Fresh and lean, used on its own and with Pinot Noir for sparkling base.

wines.note: Pale ruby, rosehip, red cherry and spice, light body and bright acidity; serve cool with salmon, duck or mushroom dishes.
Red plum, raspberry and violet with tense acidity and finer tannin than Mendoza's; with lamb, the Patagonian classic, or grilled pork.
Plummy, fresh and medium bodied; a soft red for roast chicken, pork and pasta.
Crisp and herbal from young vines, waxy and honeyed from old Sémillon; with trout, shellfish and soft cheeses.

made.viticulture: Vines are trained on vertical trellises or, in the oldest Río Negro parcels, on systems surviving from the early twentieth century, when European immigrants planted grapes among the fruit trees. Some of those vineyards, own rooted and long neglected, have become prized: the Pinot Noir planted in 1932 and 1955 at Mainque is bottled by Bodega Chacra under those dates. Windbreaks of poplar line the blocks against the westerlies, irrigation comes by flood channel or drip, and spring and autumn frost are the main hazards. Disease is rare in the dry wind, which suits organic and biodynamic farming. Harvest falls in March and April, and yields are naturally moderated by wind and cold nights.
made.winemaking: The cool climate shapes the cellar. Pinot Noir is handled gently, often with some whole bunches and little or no new oak, to keep its pale colour and perfume; Malbec is made with shorter macerations than in Mendoza and aged in used oak or concrete, for freshness over weight. Whites are fermented cool to keep their acidity, and old-vine Sémillon is sometimes aged on its lees for texture. Some houses make traditional-method sparkling wine from Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. San Patricio del Chañar was built in the 2000s by a few large estates with modern cellars, while the Alto Valle holds both historic cellars and small, natural-leaning projects.

law.classification: Patagonia works under the national framework: an Indicación Geográfica for origin, 85 per cent for a named grape and a stated vintage, and no DOC. Labels name the province, Río Negro or Neuquén, the region, Patagonia, or a valley within them; the Alto Valle del Río Negro and San Patricio del Chañar are the names a server meets most. Chubut's vineyards and the La Pampa vineyards on the Colorado river add newer origins. Altitude, so prominent on northern labels, rarely appears, because these vineyards are low.
tiers: Indicación Geográfica
The provinces Río Negro, Neuquén, La Pampa and Chubut, the regional name Patagonia, and valleys within them.
Varietal rule
85 per cent of a named grape and of a stated vintage.
