The upper Río Negro valley below the confluence, the historic heart.
Patagonia
The regional name used across the southern provinces.
Treinta y Dos, Cincuenta y Cinco
Bodega Chacra's Pinot Noirs, named for the planting years 1932 and 1955, not for vintages.

places.name: Río Negro
places.note: The province of the Alto Valle and the Valle Medio, Argentina's apple and pear orchard, where vineyards planted among the fruit trees in the early twentieth century survive as old, own-rooted parcels.

places.name: Alto Valle del Río Negro
places.note: The valley just below the confluence, around General Roca, Allen and Cipolletti, the historic wine heart of Patagonia; Humberto Canale has made wine here since the early twentieth century.

places.name: Mainque
places.note: A small town in the Alto Valle east of General Roca, where Bodega Chacra farms biodynamic Pinot Noir from vines planted in 1932 and 1955.

places.name: Valle Medio
places.note: Further downstream around Choele Choel, a smaller and newer vineyard on the same river terraces.

places.name: Neuquén
places.note: The province west of the confluence, newer to wine; most of its vineyards date from the late 1990s onward.

places.name: San Patricio del Chañar
places.note: A desert plateau north west of Neuquén city, irrigated from the Neuquén river and planted from around 2000 by large modern estates; Pinot Noir, Malbec and Merlot.

places.name: La Pampa
places.note: Vineyards on the Colorado river near Veinticinco de Mayo, at the northern edge of Patagonia, warm by day and windswept; a small, young source.

places.name: Chubut
places.note: The southern outposts, around Trevelin and El Hoyo near the Andes and Sarmiento on the steppe, beyond 42 degrees south: among the southernmost vineyards in the world, for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.

producers.name: Bodega Chacra
producers.why: Founded in 2004 at Mainque around abandoned own-rooted Pinot Noir of 1932 and 1955, farmed biodynamically; the proof that Argentina is more than Malbec.

producers.name: Humberto Canale
producers.why: The historic Alto Valle house at General Roca, making wine since the early twentieth century, known for Pinot Noir, Malbec and old-vine Sémillon.

producers.name: Bodega Noemía
producers.why: A Río Negro estate built on an old own-rooted Malbec parcel, which showed Patagonian Malbec of real finesse.

producers.name: Familia Schroeder
producers.why: A San Patricio del Chañar estate whose cellar works uncovered a dinosaur fossil, remembered in its Saurus range; Pinot Noir and Malbec.

producers.name: Bodega del Fin del Mundo
producers.why: The pioneering large estate of San Patricio del Chañar, known for Malbec, Merlot and Pinot Noir.

exam: Patagonia's vineyards are in Río Negro and Neuquén, around 38 to 39 degrees south, in irrigated river valleys.
They are low, at 200 to 400 metres: cool because of latitude and wind, not altitude.
Pinot Noir is the signature, with fresh, red-fruited Malbec and Merlot.
The Neuquén and Limay rivers meet at Neuquén city to form the Río Negro; the Alto Valle lies below the confluence.
Bodega Chacra and its Pinot Noir of 1932 and 1955 are the stock producer answer.
traps: Patagonia's vineyards are in its far north, nowhere near Tierra del Fuego; the overview map shows the crop.
The cool comes from latitude, wind and the early autumn, not from height: these vineyards lie far lower than any of the Andean fine-wine regions.
Chacra's Treinta y Dos and Cincuenta y Cinco are planting years, not vintages.
The Río Negro of Patagonia is not Uruguay's Río Negro department.
Summer days are warm here; the coolness lies in the nights and the shape of the season, so the Malbec is fresh, not thin.

cards.b: Argentina's cool south: low, windswept, irrigated valleys of Río Negro and Neuquén at 38 to 39 degrees; Pinot Noir, fresh Malbec and Merlot.
Latitude, the strong westerly wind, cold nights and an early autumn; the vineyards are low, at 200 to 400 metres, so altitude plays no part.
The Neuquén and Limay meet at Neuquén city to form the Río Negro; the Alto Valle lies just below the confluence.
Founded in 2004 at Mainque, Río Negro; biodynamic Pinot Noir from own-rooted vines of 1932 and 1955, bottled as Treinta y Dos and Cincuenta y Cinco.

cards.f: San Patricio del Chañar in one line
cards.b: Neuquén's modern zone, a desert plateau irrigated from the Neuquén river and planted from around 2000; Malbec, Pinot Noir, Merlot.
Apples and pears: canals of the early twentieth century made it Argentina's orchard, and vines were planted among the fruit trees.
Chubut: Trevelin and El Hoyo near the Andes and Sarmiento on the steppe, beyond 42 degrees south, among the southernmost vineyards in the world.

questions.q: Which two rivers meet to form the Río Negro?
questions.exp: The Neuquén and the Limay join at Neuquén city, and the Río Negro flows east through the Alto Valle. The Diamante and Atuel water San Rafael, the Mendoza and Tunuyán the rest of Mendoza, and the Colorado and Chubut are separate rivers.

questions.q: Which red grape has earned Patagonia most of its critical praise?
questions.exp: Pinot Noir, from old own-rooted Río Negro vines and newer Neuquén plantings, is Patagonia's signature. Syrah is San Juan's grape, Bonarda the everyday red of East Mendoza and Cabernet Sauvignon a blending partner almost everywhere.

questions.q: At roughly what altitude do the Río Negro and Neuquén vineyards lie?
questions.exp: Patagonia's vineyards are low, at about 200 to 400 metres, and owe their coolness to latitude and wind. The other ranges match Luján de Cuyo, the Uco Valley and Cafayate.

questions.q: Which Mainque winery bottles Pinot Noir from vines planted in 1932 as Treinta y Dos?
questions.exp: Bodega Chacra, founded in 2004 in the Río Negro valley, farms abandoned own-rooted Pinot Noir biodynamically and names its wines for the planting years, 1932 and 1955.

questions.q: Which Neuquén zone, on a plateau north west of the city, was planted from around 2000?
questions.exp: San Patricio del Chañar, irrigated from the Neuquén river, was turned from desert to vineyard by large modern estates around the turn of the century and is Neuquén's main wine zone.

questions.q: Which valley of Río Negro province, around General Roca, is Patagonia's historic wine heart?
questions.exp: The Alto Valle, the upper Río Negro valley around General Roca, Allen and Cipolletti, holds Patagonia's oldest vineyards, planted among apple and pear orchards in the early twentieth century; the Valle Medio lies further downstream.

questions.q: What chiefly keeps the Patagonian vineyards cool?
questions.exp: Latitude and the constant westerly wind cool Patagonia, whose vineyards sit only 200 to 400 metres up. Altitude cools Mendoza and Salta, Pacific fog cools coastal Chile, and the Atlantic is too far east to matter.
